summary: A humorous April 1st RFC claiming the IPng working group chose a packet format with 1696 bytes of address space. It is a joke and does not specify anything.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st RFC jokes that IPng chose an address field so large that the address became the whole message. It satirizes address-space debates and concerns about who communicates with whom.

subtitle: A satirical claim that IPng chose addresses with no room for messages.

tldr.problem: The memo jokes about debates over how much address space a future Internet protocol should use.
tldr.mechanism: It claims that IPng chose 1696 bytes of address space, a length the memo notes is a multiple of 53 and compatible with ATM architecture.
tldr.outcome: With so much space used for addresses, the fictional packet has no content left to protect, which drives the satire.

today: RFC 1776 is an Informational April 1st satire about IPng address space. It does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: The Address Is the Message
sections.content:
The memo claims that the IPng working group selected a packet format with 1696 bytes of address space. It says that length is a multiple of 53 and compatible with ATM architecture.

The joke is that packets can identify whom to talk to but leave no room for anything to say, as reflected in the title.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC pretends that an address field takes up the entire packet. The title gives the joke: the address itself becomes the message.

sections.title: Security Without Packet Content
sections.content: The memo says security experts celebrate because a packet with no content has no confidentiality or integrity concerns. It then jokes that intelligence and law-enforcement agencies focus on detecting who is communicating with whom, while service providers compete for reserved address space.
sections.plainLanguage: The satire turns the absence of message content into a supposed security solution. It shifts attention to communication patterns and competition for address allocations.

sections.title: Status of the Memo
sections.content: RFC 1776 is an informational April 1st document. It presents its claim as an IPng working-group decision. It does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an informational satire, not a real IPng packet specification.
